notes: Ruling slot 22 = Nigerian Armed Forces (SMC/FMG under Gowon, MD army sprite). Slot 13 = the federal 'super permanent secretaries'. Banned First Republic parties placed by ideology using popularity slots where fitting: NPC in 1, NNDP in 0, AG in 18 (MD places Awolowo's later UPN there), UMBC in 20, NCNC in 2, NEPU in 3. Biafran leadership (still holding an enclave on 1 Jan 1970) in 6 as anti-Western-resentful nationalism.

0.name: Nigerian National Democratic Party
0.text:
The Nigerian National Democratic Party was founded in 1964 by Chief Samuel Ladoke Akintola, premier of the Western Region, after his split from Awolowo's Action Group. Allied with the NPC, it won the rigged 1965 Western elections, which triggered riots, and was banned with all parties after the January 1966 coup in which Akintola was killed.

Its surviving leaders, such as Remi Fani-Kayode, represent a conservative Yoruba establishment loyal to the federal centre, to Britain and to the West. They favour strong government, patronage and order over mass politics. Their leverage lies in former Western Region officials, chiefs and business allies who fear Awolowo's return to supremacy.

1.name: Northern People's Congress
1.text:
The Northern People's Congress dominated the Northern Region and the federal government until the January 1966 coup, in which its leader, the Sardauna of Sokoto Sir Ahmadu Bello, and Prime Minister Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa were killed. Banned since 1966, its network of emirs, native authority officials and northern civil servants remains the most powerful in the country.

The NPC stands for northern unity, gradual change under traditional and Islamic authority, conservative economics and firm friendship with Britain and the West. Its leverage lies in the North's population, the emirate administrations and northern officers who see the federal army as the guardian of the North's place in Nigeria.

2.name: National Council of Nigerian Citizens
2.text:
The National Council of Nigerian Citizens, founded in 1944 by Herbert Macaulay and Nnamdi Azikiwe as the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons, was Nigeria's first nationalist mass party and the dominant force in the East and Mid-West. Banned since 1966, it was torn apart by the civil war; Azikiwe broke with Biafra in 1969 and now backs reconciliation.

The NCNC stands for liberal nationalism, national unity, education, enterprise and federal democracy. Its leaders, scattered between Lagos, the Mid-West and the collapsing Biafran enclave, hope to rebuild their constituencies on the federal side. Their leverage lies in their former mass base and in Azikiwe's prestige.
2.wiki: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons

3.name: Northern Elements Progressive Union
3.text:
The Northern Elements Progressive Union, founded in 1950, was the radical opposition to the emirs' rule in the North under Mallam Aminu Kano, champion of the talakawa, the commoners. Banned since 1966, its leader now sits in the Federal Executive Council as Commissioner for Communications, part of Gowon's civilian cabinet.

NEPU stands for the emancipation of commoners and women, an end to the emirs' arbitrary powers, democratic reform of the native authorities and a welfare state. Allied in the past with the NCNC, it is democratic and reformist. Its leverage lies in Kano's urban poor, teachers and petty traders, and in Aminu Kano's moral standing in the North.

4.name: Socialist Workers and Farmers Party of Nigeria
4.english: Socialist Workers and Farmers Party of Nigeria
4.text:
The Socialist Workers and Farmers Party of Nigeria was founded in 1963 by Dr Tunji Otegbeye and allied trade unionists as the country's pro-Soviet Marxist party. Banned with all parties in 1966, its cadres continue to work through the Nigerian Trade Union Congress, youth bodies and friendship societies.

The party stands for scientific socialism, nationalisation of foreign firms, oil and banks, and a planned economy in alliance with the Soviet Union, whose arms supplies to the federal side since 1967 have given it fresh arguments. Its leverage lies in organised labour in Lagos and Ibadan and in Soviet scholarships for young Nigerians.

5.name: Nigerian Trade Union Congress
5.text:
The Nigerian Trade Union Congress is the militant left-wing labour centre, formed in the early 1960s under Wahab Goodluck and affiliated with the World Federation of Trade Unions. It rivals the Western-oriented United Labour Congress and helped lead the general strike of June 1964 that shook the First Republic.

Under military rule strikes are banned, but its activists organise against wage freezes, war levies and rising prices, and call for workers' control and nationalisation. Revolutionary in rhetoric and close to the SWAFP, it rejects both the old parties and the military elite. Its leverage lies with the dockers, railwaymen and factory workers of Lagos.

6.name: The Ahiara Faithful
6.text:
The Ahiara Faithful are the leaders and cadres of secessionist Biafra, rallied around General Odumegwu Ojukwu and the Ahiara Declaration of June 1969, which proclaimed a revolutionary Biafran nation. On 1 January 1970 the enclave is collapsing under federal offensives, its people starving and its army close to surrender.

They denounce Britain and the Soviet Union for arming Lagos and the West for abandoning Biafra, and preach self-reliance, Igbo nationalism and a disciplined revolutionary society. Their leverage is fading fast, but their sense of betrayal, their diaspora networks and the memory of the 1966 massacres will outlive the war.

7.name: Araba
7.text:
Araba, Hausa for separation, was the cry of the northern officers who staged the counter-coup of July 1966, killing General Aguiyi-Ironsi and bringing Gowon to power. Its hard core, with Colonel Murtala Mohammed as the most forceful figure, now commands key formations and resents Gowon's caution.

They favour a centralised, uncompromising military state, harsh treatment of the defeated East, rapid promotion of northern officers and closer ties with the Soviet bloc that armed them when Britain hesitated. Their leverage lies in loyal battalions and in the ambition of officers who believe they won the war and should rule the peace.

8.name: Lebanese Community of Nigeria
8.text:
The Lebanese community of Nigeria, concentrated in Lagos, Kano and Ibadan, is a prosperous commercial diaspora, largely Shia from southern Lebanon, active in textiles, transport, construction and the import trade. Its families arrived in the colonial era and stayed through the civil war.

Its notables follow the reformist leadership of Imam Musa al-Sadr, elected in 1969 to head the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut, and stress civic engagement, charity and loyalty to the host state. Avoiding Nigerian politics, they cultivate officers and officials. Their leverage lies in capital, employment and their role as indispensable middlemen in the cities.

9.name: The Najaf Circle
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a small group of devout Lebanese Shia merchants and students in Kano and Lagos who look to the senior clergy of Najaf and remit religious dues to their marja'. They keep private prayer halls and send their sons to study in the Iraqi seminaries.

They insist that believers must live by religious law under clerical guidance and reject the secular style of the community's businessmen. With a few Hausa Muslims curious about Shia teachings, they form a tiny milieu, but their transnational ties carry the militant ideas of a new generation of Shia clerics into West Africa.

10.name: Jama'atu Nasril Islam
10.english: Society for the Victory of Islam
10.text:
The Society for the Victory of Islam was founded in 1962 under the patronage of Sir Ahmadu Bello and the Sultan of Sokoto as the umbrella body of northern Muslims. Since the Sardauna's death it is led by the Sultan, Sir Siddiq Abubakar III, with the emirs and senior ulama in its councils.

It promotes Islamic education, mosque-building, unity among the Sufi orders and obedience to legitimate authority, and handles relations with Saudi Arabia and the wider Muslim world. Conservative and establishment-minded, it is the religious arm of the old NPC order. Its leverage lies in Friday pulpits and the authority of the emirates.

11.name: 'Yan Tatsine
11.text:
'Yan Tatsine are the followers of Muhammadu Marwa, the Cameroonian-born preacher of Kano called Maitatsine, the one who curses, for his fiery sermons. Expelled from Kano in 1962, he has returned to the city, where he gathers poor Quranic students and migrants around a fierce message of purification.

He condemns the emirs, wealthy Muslims, radios, bicycles and Western goods as corruptions, and claims a prophetic mission that orthodox scholars call heresy. His followers reject the secular state and dream of a purified Islamic order. Few now, they thrive on the misery of Kano's swelling slums and the anger of rootless youth.

12.name: Muslim Students' Society of Nigeria
12.text:
The Muslim Students' Society of Nigeria was founded in Lagos in 1954 by Yoruba Muslim students to defend Muslim youth in a school system dominated by Christian missions. By 1970 it has branches in secondary schools and universities across the country, from Ibadan and Lagos to Zaria.

It preaches a modern, reformist Islam that unites religion and public life, criticises both Western secularism and the rigid Sufi establishment, and draws inspiration from the writers of the Muslim Brotherhood. Its leverage lies in the rising class of educated Muslims, future civil servants and professionals who seek an Islamic identity beyond ethnic loyalties.

13.name: Super Permanent Secretaries
13.text:
The Super Permanent Secretaries are the senior federal civil servants who effectively run Nigeria's government under the soldiers, among them Allison Ayida of Economic Development, Philip Asiodu of Industries and Ahmed Joda of Information. Since 1966 they have drafted decrees, planned the war economy and steered the creation of twelve states.

Technocratic and nationalist, they favour a strong centre, state-led development, indigenisation of the economy and an independent foreign policy balancing East and West. They distrust politicians and prefer prolonged military rule with civilian experts in charge. Their leverage lies in expertise and in the soldiers' dependence on their advice.

14.name: Egbe Omo Oduduwa
14.english: Society of the Descendants of Oduduwa
14.text:
The Society of the Descendants of Oduduwa is the Yoruba cultural organisation founded in London in 1945 by Obafemi Awolowo and launched in Nigeria with the backing of obas and chiefs; it gave birth to the Action Group. With parties banned, its networks survive as a forum for Yoruba leaders, elders and traditional rulers.

It stands for Yoruba unity, cultural pride, respect for the obas and a federal Nigeria in which each nationality governs its own affairs. Conservative in temper, it stands apart from the Cold War blocs. Its leverage lies in the prestige of the obas and the solidarity of Yoruba elites behind Awolowo.

15.name: Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry
15.english: Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry
15.text:
The Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry, founded in 1888, is the voice of the large trading houses, banks, oil and manufacturing companies of the federal capital, from the United Africa Company and John Holt to a growing Nigerian membership. It has weathered the war under import controls and foreign exchange rationing.

Its members want an end to wartime restrictions, open trade, a stable currency and protection of foreign investment, and they watch with concern the talk of indigenisation in the ministries. Firmly Western in orientation, they finance reconstruction schemes and cultivate officials. Their leverage lies in capital, jobs and the oil boom now beginning.
15.wiki: Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry

16.name: The Market Women of Lagos
16.text:
The Market Women of Lagos are the formidable traders of Jankara, Oyingbo and the other great markets, organised in guilds under their iyaloja, the elected head of the market women. They control the retail trade in cloth, food and household goods and handle enormous sums outside the banks.

They demand free trade, low market tolls and an end to price controls and the harassment of traders by soldiers and police, and resist any state intrusion into commerce. Long courted by the Action Group and the NCNC, they back whoever leaves them free. Their leverage lies in closing markets and filling the streets.

17.name: Nigerian Field Society
17.text:
The Nigerian Field Society, founded in 1930, gathers naturalists, foresters, teachers and scientists who study and record Nigeria's wildlife, plants and landscapes, and publishes the journal The Nigerian Field. Its members include British expatriates and a growing number of Nigerian academics at Ibadan and Zaria.

They warn against the destruction of forest reserves, the slaughter of wildlife, soil erosion in the North and pollution from the new oil industry in the Niger Delta, and call for national parks and conservation laws. Politically modest, they influence forestry officers, universities and ministries. Their leverage lies in scientific authority and international contacts.

18.name: Action Group
18.text:
The Action Group, founded in 1951 by Chief Obafemi Awolowo, governed the Western Region until its split in 1962, after which Awolowo was jailed for treasonable felony. Released by Gowon in 1966, Awolowo is now Federal Commissioner for Finance and Vice-Chairman of the Federal Executive Council, and his banned party's network is the strongest civilian force in the West.

The Action Group stands for democratic socialism, free universal education, free health care, planned development and a federal system respecting the regions. Non-aligned in outlook, it has backed the war effort through Awolowo's austerity. Its leverage lies in the Yoruba heartland, the teachers and Awolowo's growing national stature.

19.name: The Ibadan Left
19.text:
The Ibadan Left is a circle of Marxist lecturers, students and journalists at the University of Ibadan and in the Western State capital, independent of the pro-Soviet SWAFP. They study Mao, Fanon and the Cuban revolution, and run seminars, pamphlets and student societies on campus.

They argue that the civil war has served foreign oil companies and a comprador elite, and call for land reform, a mass peasant movement and a socialist path independent of both Moscow and Washington. Small and quarrelsome, they influence student leaders and young intellectuals. Their leverage lies in ideas, and in the frustration of a generation emerging from war.

20.name: United Middle Belt Congress
20.text:
The United Middle Belt Congress, led by Joseph Tarka, championed the non-Hausa, largely Christian peoples of the Middle Belt against domination by the NPC and the emirates. Its Tiv base rose in violent revolts in 1960 and 1964, and its demand for a separate region was answered by the creation of Benue-Plateau State in 1967.

Banned since 1966, the UMBC network remains a populist regional force. Tarka is now Federal Commissioner for Transport, and Middle Belt soldiers, Gowon among them, form the backbone of the infantry. It stands for minority rights, a strong federation and anti-emirate populism. Its leverage lies in the army's ranks.

21.name: Black Scorpions
21.text:
The Black Scorpions are the hard men of the 3rd Marine Commando Division, shaped by Colonel Benjamin Adekunle, the Black Scorpion, whose ruthless campaign took Port Harcourt and the coastal south before his removal from command in 1969. They regard the war as a crusade for one Nigeria.

They advocate an iron-fisted, militarised nation, collective punishment of rebels, the suppression of tribal politics and press criticism, and rule by the soldiers who saved the federation. Their creed is ultranationalism with no ideology beyond unity by force. Their leverage lies in battle-hardened units and in war heroes the public still admires.

22.name: Nigerian Armed Forces
22.text:
The Nigerian Armed Forces rule Nigeria through the Supreme Military Council and the Federal Military Government headed by Major-General Yakubu Gowon since the counter-coup of July 1966. Swollen from about 10,000 men to roughly a quarter of a million during the civil war, the army stands on the verge of victory over Biafra.

Gowon promises reconciliation, reconstruction and an eventual return to civilian rule, governing with civilian commissioners such as Awolowo. The army holds the twelve-state federation together while balancing Western and Soviet support. Its leverage is absolute: it controls the state, the oil revenues and the timetable for any political transition.

23.name: Sultanate of Sokoto
23.text:
The Sultanate of Sokoto heads the emirates of northern Nigeria as successor to the caliphate founded by Usman dan Fodio in 1804. Sultan Sir Siddiq Abubakar III, on the throne since 1938, is the spiritual leader of Nigeria's Muslims, and the emirs of Kano, Katsina and Zaria command vast native administrations.

The emirates defend Islamic custom, their courts, police and tax powers, and the social hierarchy of the North against reformers and radicals. Bereft of the NPC, they deal directly with the military government. Their leverage lies in rural loyalty and in the officers and civil servants drawn from aristocratic northern families.
